<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README, this project is a full-stack application for a user interface built to interact with a Temporal server (and its workflows). Its architecture is split between a frontend UI (built in Svelte using Vite and Tailwind) and a backend server (written in Go) that provides API endpoints, authentication, configuration, and integration with Temporal. In addition, the project contains several supporting components such as Temporal workflows/activities defined under the “temporal” directory, Docker and build configurations, and comprehensive test suites (using Playwright and Vitest) for both e2e interactions and integration testing.

Below is a step-by-step explanation on how to create an architecture/system design diagram that accurately reflects these components and their interactions:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Frontend/UI Layer: Represented by the “src” directory, including all Svelte components, pages, layouts, and styles. This layer is built with Vite and processed with tools like Tailwind CSS.
   • UI Server/Backend API: Found in the “server” directory (written in Go), which contains subdirectories for API routing, configuration, authentication, RPC, plugins, and static asset serving (for instance, “server/ui/assets” when built for the UI server).
   • Temporal Integration: The “temporal” directory shows workflows, activities, and clients that integrate the UI with Temporal. Also note that the README outlines the need for a running Temporal instance (with CLI integration) so that the UI can interact with the Temporal server.
   • External Dependencies: The Temporal CLI (downloaded on installation and/or located in PATH), Temporal Server (which must be running, either via Docker or locally), and possibly Docker infrastructure (Dockerfile, docker-compose references for containerization).
   • Build & Testing Infrastructure: 
          • Build scripts and configuration (package.json, pnpm scripts, Vite config, etc.) to create production-ready assets.
          • Test suites (e2e tests with Playwright, integration tests, and various test utilities under the “tests” folder) outlining how the components are validated.
          • Configuration files/environment variables (all the .env variants) that point to API endpoints, build targets, and Temporal port numbers.
   • Auxiliary Tools: For example, the “plugins” directory which contains plugins integrating with Vite for running the Temporal and UI servers.

2. Determine Relationships and Interactions:
   • The UI (frontend) communicates with the backend API via HTTP calls. This connection is facilitated by endpoints exposed by the Go-based server.
   • The backend API, in turn, interacts with the Temporal server to create workflows, fetch workflow statuses, and handle real-time updates. It may use RPC/gRPC or HTTP bridges based on the implementation in “server/rpc” and “server/api.”
   • The Temporal workflows and activities (from the “temporal” directory) define how business logic is executed and how events are recorded and processed.
   • Build and deployment are managed by scripts (pnpm commands, Dockerfiles, Makefiles) and CI/CD pipelines defined in the “.github” directory. Testing tools (like Playwright) are spawned by configuration in “playwright.config.ts” and tied into scripts like “pnpm test:e2e.”
   • Developers running the application locally must have a running Temporal server (via the Temporal CLI or Docker) and configure their environment (via the provided .env files) so that the UI server knows where to reach Temporal and vice versa.

3. Highlight Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Modular Separation: The project exhibits a clear separation between the UI (client-side code) and the API/backend server (Go code). There is also a distinct separation for workflow logic (Temporal workflows) and testing/deployment.
   • Configurability/Environment-Based Behavior: Multiple .env files indicate that the project is designed to support various modes (development, testing, production) with different configurations for API endpoints, ports, and build targets.
   • Plugin Architecture: The “plugins” directory indicates a modular integration point for tool-specific functionalities (e.g., vite-plugin-temporal-server.ts and vite-plugin-ui-server.ts).
   • Testing First: With extensive tests (unit, integration, and e2e), the architecture is designed for robustness and continuous validation of both UI and backend components.
   • Microservice-Friendly: While the UI and server are housed in one repository, the use of Docker, separate build commands, and distinct folders for server and workflows suggest an architecture that can be scaled or re-deployed as microservices if needed.

4. Include Relevant Technologies, Frameworks, and Libraries:
   • Frontend: Svelte, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and potentially Storybook (as evidenced by the “.storybook” directory).
   • Backend: Go (with modules and plugins for configuration, authentication, and API handling), gRPC/RPC based on the “server/rpc” folder, and possibly a standard Go HTTP server.
   • Temporal: Temporal CLI, Temporal Server, and client SDKs for connecting workflows.
   • DevOps/CI: GitHub Actions workflows, Docker configurations, and Vercel deployment configuration.
   • Testing: Playwright for e2e tests, Vitest for unit testing, and various test utilities.

5. Guidelines for Diagram Tailoring:
   – For a full-stack application like this, visually separate the frontend (client) area from the backend services. For instance, use one section for the Svelte/Vite UI and another for the Go-based API server.
   – Represent external systems clearly: include a box labeled “Temporal Server” (with further notes on CLI and Docker configuration) and perhaps an “External Storage/DB” if applicable (even if not explicitly shown, the Temporal server may have dedicated storage).
   – Draw clear directional arrows showing:
         • UI sending HTTP requests to the API.
         • API requesting/triggering workflows on the Temporal server.
         • Communication (or event streaming) from Temporal back to the API and, in turn, updating the UI.
   – Use distinct color codings or shapes:
         • Rectangles for application components.
         • Parallelograms or cylinders for external systems.
         • Dashed arrows for asynchronous or event-driven communication (such as workflow updates).
   – Label each component with its technology (e.g., “Svelte/Vite UI”, “Go API Server”, “Temporal Workflows”, “Docker/CI Pipeline”) and note any “plugins” or “configuration” components.

6. Specific Diagram Elements to Instruct on:
   • Clearly label each component (frontend, backend, temporal engine, plugins, testing framework).
   • Use directional arrows that clearly show:
         – Data flow from the UI to the backend.
         – The backend’s calls to Temporal (and receiving responses/updates).
         – Deployment workflows (e.g., from CI/CD to Docker images).
         – Testing pipelines initiating from the source code to the development server.
   • Optionally include configuration points (environment variables, buildtime configuration) that affect how components interact.
   • If space allows, add notes on infrastructure (Docker container orchestration, GitHub Actions for releases, etc.).

By capturing these details, the diagram will provide a full overview of how the Temporal UI project works: from user interaction in the Svelte frontend to API processing in the Go server and eventual orchestration with a Temporal server. This layered, modular depiction will help any principal software engineer quickly understand the interplay between core modules, external dependencies, and internal testing/build pipelines.
</explanation>
